title: Active galactic nucleus driven jet feedback in cosmologically forming cool-core galaxy clusters I: The effect of hierarchical assembly on intra-cluster medium properties
comment: 17 pages, 12 figures; submitted to A&A; comments welcome
summary: The atmospheres of cool-core galaxy clusters are excellent probes of astrophysical plasmas. However, how the interplay between assembly and active galactic nucleus (AGN) feedback leads to the observed gas profiles remains uncertain. We study the impact of hierarchical assembly on the intra-cluster medium (ICM) in cool-core galaxy clusters using hydrodynamic simulations as part of the PICO-Cluster project. We compare cosmological zoom simulations employing an explicit AGN jet model against PICO-Cluster simulations with IllustrisTNG kinetic AGN feedback, as well as against isolated galaxy cluster simulations using jet feedback. The stellar and gas fractions of our cosmological galaxy cluster simulations with jet feedback are in excellent agreement with observed galaxy clusters, and the ICM thermodynamic profiles resemble those of local cool-core galaxy clusters while those run with IllustrisTNG kinetic AGN feedback do not match these observations. In all simulations, cosmological and isolated, the AGN heating roughly balances the cooling losses, with star formation being significantly suppressed. The most notable differences between the cosmological and isolated simulations are the resulting velocity and multi-phase structure: gas at radii $> 50$ kpc is shaped by satellite galaxies rather than jet feedback originating form the central galaxy. This leads to significant differences in non-thermal pressure support, with only the cosmological simulations being consistent with recent observations. A second notable difference is the abundance of warm ($<10^5$ K) gas beyond the core region, which is absent in our isolated simulation. Our results highlight the need for taking cosmological assembly into account in comparisons of the ICM dynamics and its multi-phase nature, while self-regulation is altered by hierarchical assembly via merger-driven growth of the central supermassive black hole.

AI.tldr: Using cosmological zoom simulations with AGN jet feedback, this paper shows that hierarchical assembly (satellite galaxies, mergers) significantly impacts ICM dynamics, velocity structure, and multi-phase gas distribution in cool-core clusters, while AGN self-regulation is affected by merger-driven black hole growth.
AI.motivation: To understand how hierarchical assembly and AGN feedback jointly shape the observed thermodynamic and dynamical properties of cool-core galaxy clusters, and to determine whether isolated (non-cosmological) simulations are sufficient for modeling ICM physics.
AI.method: Cosmological zoom hydrodynamic simulations (PICO-Cluster project) with explicit AGN jet feedback, compared against IllustrisTNG kinetic AGN feedback simulations and isolated cluster simulations with jet feedback.
AI.result: Cosmological jet-feedback simulations match observed stellar/gas fractions and cool-core thermodynamic profiles; IllustrisTNG feedback does not. Cosmological and isolated simulations show similar AGN heating-cooling balance, but differ significantly in velocity structure, non-thermal pressure support, and warm gas abundance beyond core, with only cosmological runs matching observations.
AI.conclusion: Cosmological assembly is essential for accurately modeling ICM dynamics and multi-phase structure; isolated simulations miss key physics driven by satellite galaxies and merger-driven SMBH growth that alters feedback self-regulation.

title: Chinese Sunspot Drawings and Their Digitization-(VIII) Release of a Machine Readable Parameters Catalog
summary: We present a systematically revised and manually verified digital catalog of historical sunspot drawing observations from Chinese observatories, encompassing sunspot number, sunspot group number, and sunspot area measurements. This represents an updated release of China's early sunspot drawings that have been utilized in numerous published studies over the years, with ongoing refinements and corrections progressively incorporated during the course of those studies and now consolidated through a systematic round of data revision aimed at improving internal consistency and usability for the broader research community. To facilitate scientific utilization, selected comparisons with international reference sunspot data are presented, focusing on relative sunspot numbers (RSN) and sunspot group numbers (GN) from Yunnan Observatory (YNO) and Purple Mountain Observatory (PMO), while sunspot area measurements are also included in this release but are not compared with international datasets in the present work. For RSN, both raw and k-corrected values are analyzed; for GN, only raw counts are used as no dedicated correction factor exists in the Chinese records. The results demonstrate strong positive correlations, with correlation coefficients consistently exceeding 0.95 for all comparisons, confirming the reliability and scientific value of these historical records. Systematic differences are observed: raw YNO RSN values are systematically higher than SIDC by about 17.6\%, while raw PMO RSN values are about 6.0\% lower. After k-correction, YNO shifts to a 20.9\% deficit, suggesting over-correction, while PMO remains lower with a 15.5\% deficit. Notably, GN exhibits smaller systematic offsets (16.5\% for YNO and 8.5\% for PMO) and serves as a more robust index for long-term solar cycle studies.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a revised digital catalog of historical sunspot drawings from Chinese observatories (Yunnan and Purple Mountain), including sunspot number, group number, and area measurements. Comparisons with international reference data show high correlations (>0.95) but systematic offsets: YNO raw RSN is ~17.6% higher than SIDC, PMO raw RSN ~6.0% lower; after k-correction both show deficits. Group numbers exhibit smaller offsets and are recommended as more robust for long-term solar cycle studies.
AI.motivation: To systematically revise, verify, and consolidate China's historical sunspot drawing data (from YNO and PMO) into a consistent digital catalog, improving its usability for the broader research community, after years of incremental refinements in separate studies.
AI.method: Systematic revision and manual verification of historical sunspot drawings; comparison of relative sunspot numbers (raw and k-corrected) and group numbers with international reference data (SIDC); correlation and systematic offset analysis.
AI.result: Correlation coefficients >0.95 across all comparisons. Raw YNO RSN ~17.6% higher than SIDC, raw PMO RSN ~6.0% lower. After k-correction: YNO 20.9% deficit (over-correction), PMO 15.5% deficit. GN offsets smaller: 16.5% (YNO) and 8.5% (PMO).
AI.conclusion: The historical Chinese sunspot records are reliable (high correlations). Group numbers are a more robust index than RSN for long-term solar cycle studies due to smaller systematic offsets and absence of correction factor complications.

title: Constraints on the Gas Geometry Surrounding Little Red Dots through Narrow-Line Diagnostics
comment: 14 pages, 5 figures, 1 table, submitted to ApJ
summary: Little Red Dots (LRDs) are a recently identified population of high-redshift sources, with a common interpretation being accreting black holes embedded within a spherical, optically thick gas envelope. Within this framework, some models propose that the continuum arises from the dense-gas envelope, where hard ionizing radiation from the central engine is reprocessed into a stellar-like photosphere with an effective temperature of $\sim$5000 K. This implies that both the UV continuum and narrow-line emission are then powered by the host galaxy rather than an exposed central engine. To test whether this is consistent with the observed narrow-line ratios, we analyze multiple line diagnostics for a sample of $\sim$20 LRDs with high signal-to-noise NIRSpec grating spectra. We find that at least 40\% of the LRDs have line ratios pointing toward high ionization parameter and electron temperature, with a further 15\% also falling in the AGN regime for the O\textsc{i}/H$α$ diagnostic, indicative of harder ionizing radiation. These line ratios are incompatible with stellar photoionization from a star-forming host alone. This suggests lower density channels within the gas envelope through which high energy photons can escape and excite the surrounding narrow-line emitting gas. At the same time, most LRDs lack strong high-ionization line emission, with He\,\textsc{ii}/H$β$ $\lesssim0.1$, consistent with an ionizing spectrum softer than that of a standard AGN. Together, these results disfavour a uniform gas envelope with a covering fraction of unity, and instead point to a more complex geometry that gives rise to anisotropic ionizing radiation.

AI.tldr: Analysis of ~20 Little Red Dots with NIRSpec grating spectra shows that at least 40% have narrow-line ratios incompatible with pure stellar photoionization, but most lack strong high-ionization lines (HeII/Hβ ≲ 0.1). This disfavors a uniform, fully covering gas envelope and instead suggests complex geometry with anisotropic ionizing radiation and lower-density channels allowing high-energy photon escape.
AI.motivation: To test whether the observed narrow-line ratios of LRDs are consistent with the model where the continuum arises from a dense-gas envelope reprocessing central engine radiation into a stellar-like photosphere (T_eff ~ 5000 K), implying both UV continuum and narrow-line emission are host-galaxy powered rather than from an exposed AGN.
AI.method: Analyzed multiple optical/UV line diagnostics for a sample of ~20 LRDs using high signal-to-noise NIRSpec grating spectra, examining line ratio distributions relative to predictions from stellar photoionization and AGN models.
AI.result: (1) ≥40% of LRDs show line ratios indicating high ionization parameter and electron temperature; (2) ~15% fall in AGN regime for OI/Hα diagnostic; (3) Most LRDs lack strong high-ionization lines (HeII/Hβ ≲ 0.1); (4) The observed ratios are incompatible with pure stellar photoionization from a star-forming host.
AI.conclusion: A uniform gas envelope with covering fraction of unity is disfavored. Instead, the data suggest a more complex geometry with lower-density channels allowing high-energy photons to escape and excite narrow-line gas, producing anisotropic ionizing radiation with a spectrum softer than standard AGN but harder than purely stellar.

title: Evaluating the Sensitivity of the Age Inferences of Red Giant Stars to Machine Learning Methodology
comment: 17 pages, 17 figures, submitted to AAS Journals
summary: Stellar ages are vital for understanding the formation of our galaxy, but they are among the most challenging parameters to measure. Many authors address this by using machine learning models trained on stars of known age. Here we used data for 351,995 stars from Milky Way Mapper Data Release 19 to explore the sensitivity of the inferred ages to 1) neural network hyperparameters, 2) machine learning architecture, and 3) training set. We find that the resulting ages are generally insensitive to the neural network hyperparameters or the machine learning architecture, but are somewhat sensitive to the training set chosen. We also find that ages for the oldest, coolest, and lowest metallicity stars in the sample are most sensitive to the methodology used and the training set chosen. In general, our analysis suggests that even simple neural network models are sufficient for accurate age inference, but future work expanding the available training sets will be an important component of predicting reliable ages for the full galactic population.

AI.tldr: This paper tests how sensitive stellar age predictions from machine learning models are to hyperparameters, architecture, and training set, finding that only the choice of training set significantly affects results, especially for old, cool, metal-poor stars.
AI.motivation: Stellar ages are critical for understanding Galactic formation but are very difficult to measure; the authors aim to determine how reliable ML-based age predictions are by systematically testing their sensitivity to methodological choices.
AI.method: The authors use data from 351,995 stars (Milky Way Mapper Data Release 19) and train neural network models, systematically varying (1) hyperparameters, (2) architecture, and (3) training set to assess sensitivity of inferred ages.
AI.result: Ages are insensitive to hyperparameters and architecture but somewhat sensitive to training set choice. The oldest, coolest, and lowest-metallicity stars show the highest sensitivity to methodology and training set.
AI.conclusion: Simple neural network models are sufficient for accurate age inference, but expanding available training sets is critical for improving reliability, especially for the full Galactic population.

title: Red vs. Blue: How metallicity shapes black hole dynamics and mergers in dense star clusters
comment: 14 pages, 7 figures, 1 table. Submitted to ApJ, comments are welcome
summary: Dense star clusters are a well-established environment for the formation of gravitational wave sources through dynamical interactions. Recent LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA (LVK) events such as GW241011 and GW241110 provide some of the best evidence yet for a dynamical origin. However, their relatively low component masses are in tension with predictions from low-metallicity globular cluster models (which typically produce more massive black holes), hinting that these events may have originated in higher-metallicity environments. Here we present a new set of Monte Carlo star cluster simulations with refined coverage in metallicity, focusing specifically on clusters with [Fe/H] $\geq-1$, similar to the ''red'' globular cluster subpopulation observed in most galaxies. We show that metallicity has a significant effect on the mass function of black holes and black hole mergers, the total number of black hole mergers per cluster, black hole retention from natal kicks, the mass segregation time for black-hole-driven cluster dynamics, and the merger delay time distribution. We also show that high-metallicity cluster models produce low-mass hierarchical mergers consistent with the mass ratios and component masses of GW241011 and GW241110, motivating the importance of high-metallicity clusters in the astrophysical interpretation of future LVK catalogs.

AI.tldr: This paper presents new Monte Carlo simulations of high-metallicity globular clusters ([Fe/H] ≥ -1), showing they produce low-mass black hole mergers consistent with recent LVK events GW241011 and GW241110, which have component masses lower than predictions from low-metallicity cluster models.
AI.motivation: Recent LVK events (GW241011, GW241110) show evidence for a dynamical origin but have unexpectedly low component masses, in tension with low-metallicity globular cluster predictions that typically produce more massive black holes. This motivates investigating higher-metallicity clusters as alternative formation sites.
AI.method: New set of Monte Carlo star cluster simulations with refined metallicity coverage, focusing specifically on clusters with [Fe/H] ≥ -1, analogous to the "red" globular cluster subpopulation.
AI.result: Metallicity significantly affects the BH mass function, merger numbers, BH retention from natal kicks, mass segregation timescales, and merger delay time distributions. High-metallicity models produce low-mass hierarchical mergers matching the mass ratios and component masses of GW241011 and GW241110.
AI.conclusion: High-metallicity globular clusters are important for interpreting future LVK gravitational wave catalogs, as they can produce the lower-mass merger events that low-metallicity models fail to explain.

title: Discovery of a nebula associated with a high proper motion sdB star
summary: All B-type subdwarf stars (hereafter sdB) should have low flux of ionizing photons, making them incapable of producing a noticeable circumstellar photoionized shell. However, a few sdB stars have been associated with circumstellar nebulae, resembling in some cases a planetary nebula. These discoveries spark doubts about the nature of the physical processes behind the formation of the nebula. In this paper, we describe the newfound parabolic-shaped nebula associated with the high proper motion sdB star TYC 3315-1807-1. The apex of the Halpha nebula is situated approximately 0.5 arcmin in the direction of the stellar proper motion. A wider parabolic-shaped nebula is also detected in WISE W1 infrared images at 3.4 micron, whereas GALEX images show extended far-UV emission around the star within the optical and mid-IR emissions. Like most other sdB stars with associated nebulae, TYC 3315-1807-1 moves at a high-speed (102 km/s) across the Galactic plane. The low luminosity of TYC 3315-1807-1 cannot provide its wind with the momentum necessary to form and keep a bow shock. The nebula around TYC 3315-1807-1 is rather suggested to be a Mach wave partially excited by shocks and photoionization or the encounter of the star with an over-density clump in the ISM.

AI.tldr: The paper reports the discovery of a parabolic-shaped nebula around the sdB star TYC 3315-1807-1, detected in Hα, infrared (WISE W1), and far-UV (GALEX). Despite the low luminosity and ionizing flux typical of sdB stars, the nebula is unlikely a bow shock from stellar wind; instead, it is interpreted as a Mach wave from the star's high-speed motion (102 km/s) through the Galactic plane, possibly excited by shocks, photoionization, or interaction with an ISM over-density.
AI.motivation: sdB stars are expected to have low ionizing photon flux and thus should not form detectable photoionized nebulae, yet a few observed cases challenge this paradigm. This study aims to characterize the newly found nebula around TYC 3315-1807-1 and investigate the physical mechanism responsible for its formation.
AI.method: Multi-wavelength observational analysis using Hα optical imaging, WISE W1 (3.4 μm) infrared data, and GALEX far-UV images. The nebular morphology is compared with the star's proper motion direction and velocity (102 km/s).
AI.result: A parabolic-shaped Hα nebula is detected with its apex aligned with the stellar proper motion direction. A wider infrared counterpart is seen in WISE W1, and extended far-UV emission is also present. The star's low luminosity rules out a wind-driven bow shock.
AI.conclusion: The nebula around TYC 3315-1807-1 is not a bow shock but likely a Mach wave produced by the star's high-speed motion through the ISM, possibly involving shock excitation, photoionization, or interaction with an ISM over-density clump.

title: Anisotropic quenching beyond $z=1$ and its implications for preprocessing around high-redshift galaxy clusters
comment: 11 pages, 8 figures, 3 tables, submitted to PASJ
summary: Recent studies have shown that, within galaxy clusters, quenched satellite galaxies tend to be distributed preferentially along the major axis of the central galaxy, dubbed anisotropic quenching. There are various discussions about the origin of this anisotropy: some link it to active galactic nucleus activity in the central galaxy, while others attribute it to the preprocessing of galaxies within large-scale structures outside clusters. However, the definitive cause and its redshift dependence remain unclear. In this study, we investigate anisotropic quenching with 12 spectroscopically confirmed galaxy clusters at $0.9<z<1.4$. We calculate the quiescent satellite galaxy fraction as a function of orientation angle measured from the central galaxy's major axis. Although the statistical significance is modest ($\sim 2σ$), we detect anisotropic quenching in the highest redshift ever. To understand the origin of the observed anisotropy, we examine the accretion history of satellite galaxies in a cosmological simulation. We find that, in the $z=1.25$ clusters, the majority of satellite galaxies are recently ($\lesssim 2\,\mathrm{Gyr}$) infalled galaxies. In addition, the orientation angles of satellites are randomized immediately after accretion in $\sim 2\,\mathrm{Gyr}$, suggesting that only recently accreted galaxies contribute to the observed anisotropy. We adopt a semi-analytic approach that combines the accretion history of satellite galaxies with a quenching model based on a delay-then-rapid quenching framework and parameterizes both intrahalo quenching and preprocessing effects. We find that preprocessing is the dominant contributor to quenching and that the quenched fraction attributable to preprocessing is higher along the major axis than along the minor axis by $\sim20\%$, reproducing the observed anisotropic quenching signal.

AI.tldr: This study detects anisotropic quenching (preferential distribution of quenched satellites along the central galaxy's major axis) in 12 spectroscopically confirmed galaxy clusters at $0.9<z<1.4$—the highest redshift to date. Using cosmological simulations and semi-analytic modeling, the authors find that preprocessing (quenching within large-scale structures before cluster infall) is the dominant cause, with the quenched fraction along the major axis exceeding that along the minor axis by $\sim20\%$.
AI.motivation: To resolve the debated origin of anisotropic quenching in galaxy clusters and characterize its redshift dependence, as previous studies disagree on whether it stems from central AGN activity or preprocessing in large-scale structures, and its behavior at high redshift remains unexplored.
AI.method: Analyzed 12 spectroscopically confirmed clusters at $0.9<z<1.4$; measured quiescent satellite fraction vs. orientation from central galaxy major axis. Used cosmological simulations to study satellite accretion history at $z=1.25$, and constructed a semi-analytic model combining accretion history with a delay-then-rapid quenching framework parameterizing both intrahalo quenching and preprocessing.
AI.result: Detected anisotropic quenching at $\sim 2σ$ significance at the highest redshift ever. At $z=1.25$, most satellite galaxies are recently infalled ($\lesssim 2\,\mathrm{Gyr}$), and orientation randomization occurs within $\sim 2\,\mathrm{Gyr}$ post-accretion. Preprocessing dominates quenching; the quenched fraction from preprocessing is $\sim20\%$ higher along the major axis than the minor axis, reproducing the observed signal.
AI.conclusion: Preprocessing is the primary origin of anisotropic quenching in high-redshift clusters, not central AGN activity. The anisotropy arises because recently accreted galaxies, which retain their pre-infall spatial alignment and have experienced preprocessing in large-scale filaments, preferentially lie along the major axis.

title: Evolution of Stars During the Main Sequence and the Transition to the Red Giant Phase
summary:
We derive a simple analytical description for the structure and evolution of $3$--$10 M_\odot$ stars throughout main-sequence hydrogen burning. We obtain an analytical relation for the convective core mass, $\frac{M_\star}{M_c}=1+2.1\left(\frac{μ_c}{μ_e}\right)^2$, where $μ$ is the mean molecular weight of the core and envelope. Using this relation, we analytically derive the hydrogen abundance profile outside the convective core. We find that $μ(m)\propto m^{-0.7}$, and show that this profile is important for an analytical description of these stars. Within this region of variable $μ$, the temperature, density, and pressure are well approximated by power laws of radius. We derive analytical expressions for the core and stellar radii, stellar luminosity, and effective temperature as functions of $μ_c$.
  We provide a simple physical explanation for the main-sequence hook, defined by the minimum in effective temperature. We show that the hook occurs when the hydrogen mass fraction in the core is $x_c\simeq0.045$, and stress that the same convective-core burning physics governs the subsequent evolution. In that sense, at the hook hydrogen is not yet fully exhausted. During late main-sequence evolution, we find that the ratio of nuclear luminosity between the core and the surrounding hydrogen-rich shell is $\simeq4000x_c$. Hence, the main sequence terminates only once $x_c\simeq2.5\times10^{-4}$, when the surrounding layers become as luminous as the core itself and $M_c\simeq0.11 M_\star$.
  Although this terminal core mass is numerically similar to the Sch"onberg--Chandrasekhar limit, we show that the two are physically unrelated, since the core remains far from isothermal even at this stage. We validate all analytical results using MESA simulations.

AI.tldr: This paper derives an analytical description for 3–10 M☉ stars during main-sequence hydrogen burning, including convective core mass, hydrogen abundance profiles, and stellar properties. It explains the main-sequence hook and termination, showing that the terminal core mass (~0.11 M★) resembles the Schönberg–Chandrasekhar limit but is physically unrelated. All results are validated with MESA simulations.
AI.motivation: To provide a simple, physically intuitive analytical framework for intermediate-mass stars (3–10 M☉) during core hydrogen burning, explaining key features such as the main-sequence hook and the termination of the main sequence without relying solely on numerical simulations.
AI.method: The authors derive analytical relations (e.g., M★/Mc = 1 + 2.1(μc/μe)²) for convective core mass, hydrogen abundance profile (μ(m) ∝ m⁻⁰·⁷), and power-law approximations for T, ρ, P. They then derive expressions for core radius, stellar radius, luminosity, and effective temperature as functions of μc. All results are validated against MESA stellar evolution simulations.
AI.result: Key results include: (1) The main-sequence hook occurs when the core hydrogen mass fraction xc ≈ 0.045. (2) The ratio of core to shell nuclear luminosity is ≈ 4000 xc. (3) The main sequence terminates when xc ≈ 2.5×10⁻⁴ and Mc ≈ 0.11 M★. (4) Although this terminal core mass is numerically similar to the Schönberg–Chandrasekhar limit, the core remains far from isothermal, so the two are physically unrelated.
AI.conclusion: A complete analytical description of 3–10 M☉ stars throughout main-sequence evolution is possible, capturing the hook and termination physics. The Schönberg–Chandrasekhar limit does not apply because the core is not isothermal. Analytical results are in good agreement with MESA simulations.

title: Discovery of a Barred-Spiral Galaxy at $z_{spec}$ = 3.16 I: Bar Identification and Properties
summary: The formation of stellar bars is an important milestone in the secular evolution of spiral galaxies, which typically indicates the presence of a massive rotationally supported disk. Determining when these structures first appeared in the early universe is crucial to constraining the timeline of galactic disk assembly. Here, we report the discovery of COSMOS-74706, a barred spiral galaxy at $z_{spec} = 3.159$. Imaging of COSMOS-74706 with JWST/NIRCam indicates a disk-like morphology and spiral structure with an elongated central feature aligned between the spiral arms, most conspicuously visible in the F200W, F277W, and F356W filters. Three independent methods all support the presence of a bar: visual inspection of residuals from Sérsic-profile fitting shows a linear structure, isophotal ellipse-fitting displays characteristic profiles of ellipticity and position angle consistent with a bar signature, and Fourier decomposition of the galaxy produces a central bisymmetric mode above a threshold strength calibrated to $z=1-3$ barred spirals. Leveraging archival Keck/MOSDEF spectroscopy overlapping with a blue clump on the edge of the galaxy, a robust redshift is inferred, with photometric constraints indicating that this structure lies at the same redshift as the main spiral. This spectroscopic evidence, placing an unlensed barred spiral at $z>3$ supports the idea that galaxies with rotationally supported disks and disk-halo properties that are conducive to bar formation were already in place within 2 Gyr after the Big Bang.

AI.tldr: Discovery of COSMOS-74706, a barred spiral galaxy at redshift z=3.159 (within 2 Gyr after the Big Bang), identified via JWST/NIRCam imaging and confirmed by three independent bar-detection methods (Sérsic residuals, isophotal ellipse-fitting, Fourier decomposition), with spectroscopic redshift from Keck/MOSDEF. This pushes the earliest known barred spiral galaxy back to a time when rotationally supported disks were already present.
AI.motivation: To constrain the timeline of galactic disk assembly by determining when stellar bars—indicators of massive rotationally supported disks—first appeared in the early universe.
AI.method: JWST/NIRCam imaging of COSMOS-74706 at z=3.159; three independent bar-detection methods (visual inspection of Sérsic residuals, isophotal ellipse-fitting for ellipticity/position angle profiles, Fourier decomposition for bisymmetric mode strength); archival Keck/MOSDEF spectroscopy for robust redshift determination; photometric consistency checks.
AI.result: A barred spiral galaxy (COSMOS-74706) identified at z=3.159, with all three bar-detection methods consistently supporting the presence of a bar structure; spectroscopic evidence confirms it lies at the same redshift as the main spiral, placing an unlensed barred spiral at z>3.
AI.conclusion: Rotationally supported disks with properties conducive to bar formation existed within 2 Gyr after the Big Bang, pushing back the timeline for the emergence of barred spiral galaxies to z>3.

title: Beyond the Tayler instability: A new global instability of toroidal magnetic fields in stars
comment: 44 pages, 12 figures, 3 tables, accepted in Phys. Rev. D
summary: Stellar toroidal magnetic fields are known to be unstable to the Tayler instability. Here we demonstrate the existence of a complementary current-driven instability of essentially arbitrary toroidal-field configurations in stably stratified nonrotating stars with the following properties: (i) in ideal magneto-hydrodynamics, it grows on the Alfvén timescale $τ_{\rm A}$; (ii) under certain conditions, it may reveal itself by driving shellular differential rotation about an arbitrary axis perpendicular to the magnetic-field symmetry axis; (iii) it is large-scale in the angular directions $θ$ and $\varphi$, and develops at radial wave-numbers $k \lesssim \mathcal{N}τ_{\rm A}/R$, where $\mathcal{N}$ is the Brunt-Väisälä frequency and $R$ is the stellar radius. Thus, unlike the Tayler instability, the proposed instability is intrinsically global. Consequently, it may be less susceptible to dissipative suppression than the Tayler instability and can prevail over it in some regimes. This instability may have broad implications for magnetic field generation in stars and could modify scenarios of magnetic field amplification within the Tayler-Spruit dynamo, contributing to models of efficient angular-momentum transport and chemical mixing in stellar interiors.

AI.tldr: This paper identifies a new global, current-driven instability in toroidal magnetic fields within stably stratified, nonrotating stars. Unlike the Tayler instability, it grows on Alfvén timescales, drives shellular differential rotation, is large-scale in angular directions, and may be less susceptible to dissipative suppression, with implications for stellar dynamos, angular-momentum transport, and chemical mixing.
AI.motivation: To demonstrate the existence of a complementary current-driven instability of toroidal-field configurations in stably stratified nonrotating stars that is global in nature and may be less susceptible to dissipative suppression than the known Tayler instability, with potential implications for magnetic field generation and angular-momentum transport in stellar interiors.
AI.method: Theoretical analysis using ideal magneto-hydrodynamics to characterize a current-driven instability in toroidal magnetic fields in stably stratified, nonrotating stars, examining its growth rate (Alfvén timescale), spatial structure (large-scale in angular directions, radial wave-numbers constrained by Brunt-Väisälä frequency and stellar radius), and resulting dynamics (shellular differential rotation).
AI.result: (i) The instability grows on the Alfvén timescale in ideal MHD; (ii) it can drive shellular differential rotation about an arbitrary axis perpendicular to the magnetic-field symmetry axis; (iii) it is large-scale in angular directions and develops at radial wave-numbers k ≲ N τ_A / R; (iv) it is intrinsically global, unlike the Tayler instability, making it less susceptible to dissipative suppression.
AI.conclusion: This global current-driven instability may prevail over the Tayler instability in some regimes, have broad implications for magnetic field generation in stars, modify scenarios of magnetic field amplification within the Tayler-Spruit dynamo, and contribute to models of efficient angular-momentum transport and chemical mixing in stellar interiors.

title: Discovery of a Barred-Spiral Galaxy at $z_{spec}$ = 3.16 II. The Star Formation History
summary: We present a detailed analysis of a massive barred galaxy at $z_{spec}=3.1591$ using deep multi-band imaging from HST and JWST. For the first time, we resolve its morphology and stellar structures thanks to the JWST/NIRCam NIR and MIR photometry. The galaxy possesses two distinct components with significantly different colors. Through careful image decomposition and masking, we isolate and characterize the flux contribution from each component. The galaxy exhibits a clear spiral morphology, and in a separate companion paper, we present evidence suggesting the presence of a stellar bar. Based on spatially resolved spectral energy distribution modeling with Prospector, we derive the star formation history and other physical properties of the bar and the surrounding regions. The total stellar mass of the galaxy is constrained as $\log(M_*/M_{\odot}) = 10.63\pm0.13$. We find that the bar region contains around 30% of the total stellar mass, but only accounts for around 8% of the recent star formation rate. The region containing the potential bar shows a significantly older mass-weighted stellar age, supporting the inside-out scenario for galaxy formation, and providing tentative evidence for bar quenching in the early stage. The quick onset of a stellar bar at this redshift requires a low dark matter fraction, suggesting the baryon-dominated nature of high-$z$ massive galaxies, and offering rare insight into galaxy evolution at around two billion years after the Big Bang.

AI.tldr: A massive barred galaxy at z=3.1591 is analyzed using HST and JWST data. JWST/NIRCam resolves its two-component structure: a bar region containing ~30% of stellar mass but only ~8% of recent star formation, with older stellar ages supporting inside-out formation and early bar quenching. The bar's quick onset implies a low dark matter fraction, indicating baryon-dominated high-z massive galaxies.
AI.motivation: To resolve and characterize the morphology and stellar structures of a massive barred galaxy at high redshift (z~3.16) using deep multi-band imaging from HST and JWST, providing the first detailed look at such early bar formation and its implications.
AI.method: Deep multi-band HST and JWST/NIRCam imaging, image decomposition and masking to isolate two color-distinct components, spatially resolved SED modeling with Prospector to derive star formation history and physical properties.
AI.result: Total stellar mass log(M*/M☉)=10.63±0.13. Bar region has ~30% of stellar mass but only ~8% of recent SFR. Bar region shows older mass-weighted stellar age. Evidence for early bar quenching and baryon-dominated nature at high redshift.
AI.conclusion: The findings support inside-out galaxy formation, suggest early bar quenching occurs at z~3, and imply a low dark matter fraction (baryon dominance) in high-z massive galaxies, offering rare insights into galaxy evolution ~2 Gyr after the Big Bang.

title: The PICO-Cluster Project: presenting the galaxy cluster sample and studying magnetic field growth, Faraday rotation and Braginskii heating
comment: 33 pages, 20 figures, submitted to MNRAS, project webpage available at http://pico-cluster.aip.de/
summary: Galaxy clusters constitute a microcosm of the Universe and offer a unique laboratory for studying plasma astrophysics, encompassing processes such as cosmic-ray acceleration and non-thermal radio emission, turbulence, weakly collisional plasma physics, and transformative mechanisms in galaxy evolution. To investigate these phenomena, we introduce the PICO-Cluster project, studying 'Plasmas In COsmological Clusters' using a suite of high-resolution cosmological zoom-in simulations of massive galaxy clusters with masses $\gtrsim10^{15}$M$_\odot$ selected from a parent simulation box with a comoving side length of 1 $h^{-1}$Gpc. In this work, we present 24 baseline simulations performed with the moving-mesh AREPO code and the IllustrisTNG galaxy formation model, achieving a baryonic mass resolution of up to $1.4\times10^{6}\mathrm{M}_\odot$. The initial conditions are carefully designed to exclude low-resolution particle contamination within the high-resolution region; as a result, all clusters remain free of such contamination out to at least 2.7 $R_{200}$ at all times. Our galaxy and cluster properties agree with recent simulations and many observational constraints, including scaling relations and thermodynamic profiles. The magnetic energy within the cluster is numerically converged once the small-scale dynamo has saturated, yielding a remarkably tight volume-averaged plasma-beta of $β\approx100$ inside $R_{200}$ across our sample after redshift $z\sim1.2$. Faraday rotation measure profiles, which trace the line-of-sight magnetic field and electron density, decline with cylindrical radius; notably, the mean decreases more rapidly than the root-mean-square due to the increasing relative contribution of galaxies at larger radii. Finally, viscous heating rates in Braginskii theory are highly intermittent and, on average, approach radiative cooling rates in the cluster outskirts.

AI.tldr: The PICO-Cluster project uses 24 high-resolution cosmological zoom-in simulations of massive galaxy clusters (≥10¹⁵ M☉) with the AREPO code and IllustrisTNG model to study plasma astrophysics. Key findings include: contamination-free initial conditions out to ≥2.7 R₂₀₀, numerically converged magnetic energy with saturated small-scale dynamo yielding β≈100 inside R₂₀₀ after z~1.2, declining Faraday rotation measure profiles with radius, and viscous heating rates approaching radiative cooling in cluster outskirts.
AI.motivation: Galaxy clusters provide a unique laboratory for studying plasma astrophysics (cosmic-ray acceleration, turbulence, non-thermal emission, weakly collisional plasma physics, galaxy evolution), but high-resolution simulations of massive clusters with realistic magnetic fields and plasma physics are lacking.
AI.method: Suite of 24 high-resolution cosmological zoom-in simulations using moving-mesh AREPO code with IllustrisTNG galaxy formation model; clusters selected from a 1 h⁻¹Gpc parent box; baryonic mass resolution up to 1.4×10⁶ M☉; careful initial conditions to avoid low-resolution particle contamination.
AI.result: Clusters are contamination-free out to ≥2.7 R₂₀₀; galaxy/cluster properties agree with observations; magnetic energy converges after small-scale dynamo saturation with volume-averaged β≈100 inside R₂₀₀ after z~1.2; Faraday RM profiles decline with radius (mean faster than RMS due to galaxy contribution); Braginskii viscous heating is intermittent and approaches radiative cooling in outskirts.
AI.conclusion: The PICO-Cluster suite provides a robust numerical framework for studying plasma astrophysics in massive galaxy clusters, with converged magnetic field properties and realistic thermodynamic profiles that match observations. The results highlight the importance of small-scale dynamo saturation, the role of galaxies in magnetic field structure, and the potential of viscous heating in cluster outskirts.

title: Characterising magnetic fields at the onset of star cluster formation: From giant molecular clouds to infrared dark clumps
comment: Accepted for publication in MNRAS; 41 pages, 37 figures, 13 tables (including appendices)
summary: The role of magnetic fields in the observed inefficiency of star formation in Galactic molecular clouds is a widely debated topic, with the past decade seeing an explosion of observational characterisation of magnetic fields in star-forming regions. However, few have studied the spatial evolution of magnetic fields from entire molecular clouds down to parsec-size cluster-forming clumps. In this work, the plane-of-sky morphology of the magnetic fields of eight infrared dark clumps and their parent molecular clouds are derived from Planck and JCMT POL-2 polarisation data (including some from the BISTRO survey). We also use this data to test multiple methods of calculating B-field strengths. Our study shows that the morphologies of magnetic fields in clumps and their parent molecular clouds systematically, and significantly, differ, supported by a line-of-sight correction of the cloud-scale magnetic fields using the velocity gradient technique. We find a strong correlation between gas velocity dispersion and the alignment of magnetic field lines with column density gradients from scales of tens of parsecs to a few parsecs. This correlation is clear evidence of a link between the kinematic properties of the gas and the dynamical importance of magnetic fields. Conversely, the higher magnetic field strengths we measure on cloud scale compared to clump scale contradict magnetic flux conservation and thus highlight the unreliability of such measurements. Altogether, our analysis supports a picture in which magnetic fields have little impact on the dynamical evolution of cluster-forming clumps but do play a role in providing support on larger scales.

AI.tldr: This study analyzes magnetic field morphologies in eight infrared dark clumps and their parent molecular clouds using Planck and JCMT POL-2 data, finding that magnetic field structures systematically differ between cloud and clump scales, with a strong correlation between gas velocity dispersion and field alignment with column density gradients, supporting a model where magnetic fields are dynamically important on cloud scales but not on clump scales.
AI.motivation: To resolve the debate about the role of magnetic fields in the observed inefficiency of star formation by studying the spatial evolution of magnetic fields from entire molecular clouds down to parsec-size cluster-forming clumps.
AI.method: Plane-of-sky magnetic field morphologies of eight infrared dark clumps and their parent molecular clouds derived from Planck and JCMT POL-2 polarisation data (including BISTRO survey data); line-of-sight correction applied via velocity gradient technique; multiple methods tested for calculating B-field strengths.
AI.result: Magnetic field morphologies systematically and significantly differ between clumps and their parent molecular clouds; strong correlation found between gas velocity dispersion and alignment of magnetic field lines with column density gradients from tens of parsecs to a few parsecs; higher magnetic field strengths measured on cloud scale than clump scale, contradicting magnetic flux conservation.
AI.conclusion: Magnetic fields have little impact on the dynamical evolution of cluster-forming clumps but do play a role in providing support on larger (cloud) scales; the correlation between gas kinematics and magnetic field alignment provides clear evidence linking kinematic properties to the dynamical importance of magnetic fields.

title: First measurement of narrow-line flux ratios for a lensed quasar with JWST/NIRSpec IFS
comment: 18 pages, 9 figures, submitted to Physical Review D
summary: Strong gravitational lensing is a powerful probe of dark matter (DM) structure on subgalactic scales: in particular, statistics of flux-ratio anomalies (discrepancies between mass model predictions and observed flux ratios) in quadruply imaged quasars are sensitive to perturbations by low-mass DM halos down to $\sim 10^6 M_\odot$. Studies leveraging these anomalies require high-quality flux-ratio measurements from an emission region insensitive to stellar microlensing. In this paper, we present the first measurement of narrow-line flux ratios for a gravitationally lensed quasar using JWST/NIRSpec with Integral Field Spectroscopy (IFS), targeting the well-studied system RXJ1131$-$1231. Flux ratios are extracted from the [S III] 9071/9533 $Å$ narrow-line doublet - the first use of this doublet for substructure studies - by performing a full lens model reconstruction to isolate the unresolved nuclear emission from extended narrow-line emission. The resulting spectra are jointly modeled using $\texttt{lensqso-specfit}$, a publicly available software package introduced in this work for the simultaneous spectral fitting of multiple lensed quasar images. We achieve $\sim$ 5% uncertainties on the flux ratios, comparable to the precision of JWST/MIRI warm dust measurements, and detect a clear anomaly in the cusp images relative to a standard smooth lens model. Our results are in good agreement with previous narrow-line measurements and broadly consistent with JWST/MIRI warm dust flux ratios, with marginal ($\sim 2-3σ$) deviations. We demonstrate how such shifts between differently sized emission regions may be enhanced by small ($\sim 10$ pc) spatial offsets. Our method is generalizable to other systems with existing or future IFS observations, and the combination of narrow-line and warm dust flux ratios offers a new avenue for improving DM constraints with flux-ratio anomaly statistics.

AI.tldr: This paper presents the first JWST/NIRSpec IFS measurement of narrow-line flux ratios (using the [S III] doublet) for the lensed quasar RXJ1131-1231, achieving ~5% precision, detecting a clear anomaly in cusp images, and introducing the open-source software package lensqso-specfit for joint spectral fitting of lensed quasar images.
AI.motivation: Strong gravitational lensing flux-ratio anomalies probe low-mass DM halos down to ~10^6 M⊙, but require high-quality flux-ratio measurements from emission regions insensitive to stellar microlensing. Existing measurements lack sufficient resolution or are affected by microlensing, motivating the need for narrow-line flux ratios from JWST/NIRSpec IFS.
AI.method: JWST/NIRSpec Integral Field Spectroscopy (IFS) was used to observe RXJ1131-1231. Flux ratios were extracted from the [S III] 9071/9533 Å narrow-line doublet via full lens model reconstruction to isolate unresolved nuclear emission from extended narrow-line emission. Spectra were jointly modeled using lensqso-specfit, a new publicly available software package for simultaneous spectral fitting of multiple lensed quasar images.
AI.result: Achieved ~5% flux ratio uncertainties, comparable to JWST/MIRI warm dust precision. Detected a clear anomaly in cusp images relative to a standard smooth lens model. Results agree with previous narrow-line measurements and broadly with MIRI warm dust ratios, with marginal (~2-3σ) deviations.
AI.conclusion: The method is generalizable to other lensed systems with IFS data. Combining narrow-line and warm dust flux ratios offers a new avenue for improving dark matter constraints via flux-ratio anomaly statistics. Small (~10 pc) spatial offsets between differently sized emission regions may explain observed shifts.

title: A Strongly Lensed Ultra-faint Arc at $z \approx 10$ with an F200W excess in Abell S1063
summary: Strong gravitational lensing provides a powerful route to probing intrinsically faint galaxies during the first few hundred million years of cosmic history. In this Letter, we report the identification of GAR10, a highly magnified F115W-dropout galaxy at $z\approx10$ in the Abell S1063 cluster field, using deep JWST/NIRCam imaging from the GLIMPSE and GO-1840 programs. The source shows an unusually blue ultraviolet (UV) continuum and a significant F200W excess relative to adjacent bands. Under our high-magnification lensing solution, we infer a median magnification of $μ=43^{+78}_{-20}$, corresponding to an intrinsic UV magnitude of $M_{\rm UV}\approx-15.8$. We use exploratory Prospector SED modeling to examine two physically motivated interpretations of the observed photometry. In Case I, GAR10 is described by an extremely metal-poor, continuum-dominated stellar population at $z=10.75_{-0.34}^{+0.41}$, with a blue UV slope of $β=-2.92\pm0.12$ and a low metallicity of $\log(Z/Z_\odot)=-3.56_{-0.85}^{+0.65}$, consistent with an extremely metal-poor or Pop III-like continuum-dominated interpretation under the adopted priors. In Case II, GAR10 is interpreted as an extremely young (1--3 Myr), high-ionization galaxy at $z=10.45_{-0.21}^{+0.11}$, in which the F200W excess is produced by intense rest-frame UV emission lines, including CIV, HeII, and CIII]. Both cases can partially reproduce the current photometry within the adopted priors, but they imply distinct ionizing sources, enrichment histories, and possible contributions to cosmic reionization. GAR10 therefore represents a rare laboratory for studying ultra-faint galaxy formation at cosmic dawn. Future JWST/NIRSpec spectroscopy will be essential to distinguishing between the steep continuum and emission-line origins of the F200W excess.

AI.tldr: JWST/NIRCam imaging identifies GAR10, a highly magnified (μ≈43) z≈10 galaxy in the Abell S1063 cluster. It exhibits an unusually blue UV continuum and F200W excess. Two models fit the data: (I) an extremely metal-poor, continuum-dominated stellar population (Pop III-like), or (II) a very young (1–3 Myr) galaxy with strong rest-frame UV emission lines (CIV, HeII, CIII]). Spectroscopy is needed to discriminate between these origins.
AI.motivation: To identify and characterize ultra-faint galaxies at z≈10, enabling the study of intrinsically faint sources during cosmic dawn through strong gravitational lensing.
AI.method: Deep JWST/NIRCam imaging from GLIMPSE and GO-1840 programs; high-magnification lensing solution (μ=43⁺⁷⁸₋₂₀); Prospector SED modeling with two physically motivated priors (extremely metal-poor stellar population vs. young galaxy with strong emission lines).
AI.result: GAR10 is a F115W-dropout at z≈10 with M_UV≈-15.8, blue UV slope β=-2.92±0.12, and an unusually blue UV continuum with significant F200W excess. Two competing models both partially reproduce the photometry but imply very different physical origins.
AI.conclusion: GAR10 is a rare laboratory for studying ultra-faint galaxy formation at cosmic dawn. Future JWST/NIRSpec spectroscopy is essential to distinguish between the steep continuum and emission-line interpretations of the F200W excess.

title: The MASSIVE SURVEY XXI: Local Variations in the Stellar Initial Mass Function of MASSIVE Early-Type Galaxies
summary: Extensive evidence suggests that the stellar initial mass function (IMF) varies among early-type galaxies (ETGs), but spatially resolved studies within individual galaxies are limited in sample size. We investigate radial variations in the low-mass ($\leq1M_{\odot}$) IMF and its connection to stellar populations in 37 nearby massive ETGs from the MASSIVE survey. Using high-quality Magellan/LDSS-3 long-slit spectroscopy spanning $0.4μ$m$-1.01μ$m, we extract spectra in radial bins reaching outermost radii of 0.2-1.1Re across the sample. We find that the IMF becomes less bottom-heavy with increasing radius in most galaxies. The sample-averaged IMF mismatch parameter, $α_{\rm IMF}=(M/L)/(M/L)_{\rm Kroupa}$, decreases from 2.16 within Re/8 to 1.74 in the Re/4-Re/2 bin, with galaxy-to-galaxy scatters of 0.50 and 0.42, respectively. Thus, the average IMF remains more bottom-heavy than Kroupa and approximately Salpeter-like or more bottom-heavy over these radii. The radial gradients of $\log(α_{\rm IMF})$ anti-correlate with the central value of $α_{\rm IMF}$, indicating that galaxies with more bottom-heavy central IMFs decline more steeply toward less bottom-heavy, approximately Salpeter-like values at larger radii. We find mild positive local correlations between $α_{\rm IMF}$ and stellar metallicity, but no significant local correlation with [Mg/Fe] or [Na/Fe]. Together with the approximately flat profiles of several [$α$/Fe], this suggests that IMF variation in massive ETGs is more closely linked to metallicity than to the star-formation timescale traced by [$α$/Fe]. Finally, the radial variation in stellar $M/L_r$ is dominated by the IMF gradient rather than by the stellar-population gradient. A fixed Kroupa IMF underestimates stellar masses by factors of 1.7 and 1.5 within Re/2 and Re in massive ETGs.

AI.tldr: This study analyzes radial variations in the low-mass stellar initial mass function (IMF) across 37 massive early-type galaxies from the MASSIVE survey. Using long-slit spectroscopy, the authors find that IMF becomes less bottom-heavy with increasing radius, with the average IMF mismatch parameter decreasing from 2.16 (within Re/8) to 1.74 (Re/4-Re/2). Radial gradients anti-correlate with central IMF values, and IMF variations correlate more strongly with metallicity than with alpha-element ratios. The IMF gradient dominates radial variations in stellar mass-to-light ratio.
AI.motivation: While IMF variations are known to exist among early-type galaxies, spatially resolved studies within individual galaxies remain limited in sample size. This work aims to systematically investigate radial IMF gradients across a large sample (37 galaxies) to understand the connection between IMF and stellar population properties.
AI.method: The authors use high-quality Magellan/LDSS-3 long-slit spectroscopy (0.4μm–1.01μm) for 37 massive ETGs from the MASSIVE survey. Spectra are extracted in radial bins reaching 0.2–1.1 Re. The IMF is parameterized via the mismatch parameter α_IMF = (M/L)/(M/L)_Kroupa, derived from stellar population synthesis modeling.
AI.result: IMF becomes less bottom-heavy with increasing radius in most galaxies. Sample-averaged α_IMF decreases from 2.16 (inner bin) to 1.74 (outer bin). Radial gradients of log(α_IMF) anti-correlate with central α_IMF. Mild positive local correlations exist between α_IMF and stellar metallicity, but no significant correlation with [Mg/Fe] or [Na/Fe]. IMF gradient dominates radial M/L_r variation over stellar-population gradients. Fixed Kroupa IMF underestimates stellar masses by factors of 1.7 (within Re/2) and 1.5 (within Re).
AI.conclusion: IMF variation in massive ETGs is more closely linked to metallicity than to star-formation timescale (traced by [α/Fe]). The radial IMF gradient is the primary driver of the radial variation in stellar mass-to-light ratio, and using a fixed Kroupa IMF leads to significant underestimation of stellar masses in these galaxies.

title: Radial gradients revealed by mutliscale outflows from down-the-barrel spectroscopy toward a quasar at redshift 3.4
comment: Accepted for publication in ApJ, 12 pages, 7 figures
summary: Active galactic nucleus(AGN) feedback is a key ingredient in galaxy formation models and simulations. From an observational point of view, however, the channels of AGN feedback coupling to the interstellar medium (ISM) and circumgalactic medium (CGM) and hence the impact on galaxy evolution, are largely uncertain and remain fiercely debated, due primarily to the huge gap from nuclear to CGM scales. Here we present multi-epoch, down-the-barrel spectroscopy toward a luminous quasar at $z=3.409$ over two decades, which reveals multiscale outflows expanding from nuclear to CGM scales along with characteristic radial gradients. Most strikingly, the trends of trough depth across three different-scale, freely expanding outflows are opposite between N V and C IV, regardless of the spectral normalization and short-term variability, leading to a tenable gradient of N/C and signaling a critical transition from ejective feedback on small scales to regulative feedback on large scales. Our observations of this quasar offer valuable diagnostics to explore the realistic wind-ISM/CGM coupling, one of the most challenging tasks in state-of-the-art simulations of feedback.

AI.tldr: Multi-epoch spectroscopy of a z=3.409 quasar reveals multiscale outflows from nuclear to CGM scales with opposite N V and C IV trough depth gradients, indicating a transition from ejective to regulative AGN feedback.
AI.motivation: The observational channels of AGN feedback coupling to the ISM and CGM, and its impact on galaxy evolution, remain largely uncertain due to the huge gap from nuclear to CGM scales. This study aims to bridge that gap.
AI.method: Multi-epoch, down-the-barrel spectroscopy toward a luminous quasar at z=3.409 over two decades, analyzing absorption troughs (N V and C IV) across different-scale outflows.
AI.result: Opposite radial gradients in N V and C IV trough depths are observed across outflows, independent of spectral normalization and short-term variability, indicating a gradient in N/C abundance and a transition from ejective to regulative feedback.
AI.conclusion: These observations provide valuable diagnostics for exploring realistic wind-ISM/CGM coupling, a challenging task for state-of-the-art feedback simulations.

title: Dual-disk galaxies and thermal states of circumgalactic medium
comment: 11 pages, 6 figures, published in the Open Journal of Astrophysics
summary: Disk galaxies often have dual-disk structures composed of thin disks and thick disks. Recent observations reveal that such duality is ubiquitous across broad galaxy mass and cosmic time. It is suggested that more massive galaxies have smaller mass fractions of thick disks and undergo a transition from thick (or single) disk states to dual-disk states at earlier times. Previous studies suggest that the circumgalactic medium (CGM) in halos above the critical mass is heated by the development of stable shocks and feedback from active galactic nuclei. It has been argued that this thermal change of the CGM causes the transition of the accretion of CGM from the fast cold mode to the slow hot mode driven by the radiative cooling of heated CGM. We consider here the hypothesis that the cold and hot modes promote the formation of thick and thin disks, respectively. Previous theoretical studies showed that this hypothesis explains the age and chemical bimodality of the Milky Way disk as well as the mass dependence of disk duality observed for local galaxies. Using simple galaxy evolution models, we show that this hypothesis also reproduces the thick-to-thin disk mass ratios observed for high-redshift galaxies up to $z=2$. Earlier transition to dual disks in more massive galaxies is explained as the outcome of earlier crossing of the critical halo mass by more massive halos. The caveat here is that this interpretation is not applicable to bulge-dominated galaxies at the high-mass end because present models do not include galaxy mergers, which likely act as the primary route to bulge formation. It should also be noted that the link between the disk duality and gas accretion modes may be indirect and multiple processes may transform accreted material into different types of disks in real galaxies.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes that the formation of thick and thin disks in galaxies is driven by cold and hot gas accretion modes from the circumgalactic medium (CGM), respectively. Using simple galaxy evolution models, the authors show this hypothesis reproduces observed thick-to-thin disk mass ratios up to redshift z=2, with more massive galaxies transitioning to dual-disk states earlier due to earlier crossing of a critical halo mass threshold.
AI.motivation: To explain the ubiquitous dual-disk structure (thin + thick disks) observed across galaxy mass and cosmic time, and to understand why more massive galaxies have smaller thick disk mass fractions and transition to dual-disk states earlier.
AI.method: Simple galaxy evolution models that link CGM accretion modes (cold vs. hot, driven by CGM shock heating and AGN feedback above a critical halo mass) to disk formation: cold mode forms thick disks, hot mode forms thin disks. Models compare predicted thick-to-thin disk mass ratios with observations up to z=2.
AI.result: The hypothesis successfully reproduces the observed thick-to-thin disk mass ratios for high-redshift galaxies up to z=2. Earlier transitions to dual-disk states in more massive galaxies are explained by their earlier crossing of the critical halo mass threshold.
AI.conclusion: The cold/hot accretion mode hypothesis for thick/thin disk formation is consistent with high-redshift observations. However, the model does not apply to bulge-dominated galaxies where mergers dominate, and the link between disk duality and accretion modes may be indirect with multiple processes involved.

title: A First Measurement of Circumgalactic Dust Reddening from Only 4.6 deg$^2$ of the Rubin Observatory's DP1
summary: We present the first measurement of circumgalactic dust reddening from the Vera C. Rubin Observatory, using only 4.6 deg$^2$ of ComCam Data Preview 1 - roughly $0.03\%$ of the final LSST footprint. Using photometric redshifts, we stack background-galaxy colors around foreground-galaxy positions and detect a chromatic reddening profile from $r_\perp \simeq 10$ kpc to $1$ Mpc. Interpreting average $E(g-z)$ with a Milky Way extinction curve, we find $A_V = (1.2 \pm 0.4) \times 10^{-1} (r_\perp / 20\,\mathrm{kpc})^{-1.8 \pm 0.4}$ within $120$ kpc. The amplitude and radial dependence agree with earlier SDSS, KiDS, and DES results despite the $\sim1000\times$ smaller survey area and a foreground sample extending 3-6 mag fainter and 1-2 dex lower in stellar mass. The innermost 10-15 kpc bin reaches $A_V \simeq 0.3$ mag, comparable to high-latitude extinction through the Milky Way disk near the Solar circle; the steep power-law slope implies a dust distribution that does not simply trace the halo-gas profile. Splitting by rest-frame $g-r$ shows stronger extinction around red foreground galaxies (rest-frame $g-r > 0.5$), although the blue subsample is too noisy to establish a significant color dependence. This red sample, with median halo mass $5 \times 10^{11}\,M_\odot$, shows substantially more reddening within 50 kpc than previously measured around more massive LRGs and implies a dust-to-stellar-mass ratio of $\sim 1\%$, nearly saturating the dust budget allowed by stellar metal yields. These pathfinder data demonstrate LSST's promise for high-precision galaxy-dust measurements across galaxy mass, environment, and redshift.

AI.tldr: Using only 0.03% of the final LSST footprint (4.6 deg² of ComCam Data Preview 1), the authors measure circumgalactic dust reddening for the first time with Rubin data. Stacking background galaxy colors around foreground galaxies, they detect a reddening profile from ~10 kpc to 1 Mpc with A_V ~0.3 mag in the innermost bin, consistent with earlier SDSS/KiDS/DES results despite vastly smaller area and fainter foreground samples. Red galaxies show stronger extinction, with dust-to-stellar mass ratio ~1%, saturating the stellar metal yield budget.
AI.motivation: To demonstrate LSST's capability for measuring circumgalactic dust reddening at high precision across galaxy mass, environment, and redshift, using early Rubin data.
AI.method: Stacking background-galaxy colors (E(g-z)) around foreground galaxies using photometric redshifts from 4.6 deg² of Rubin ComCam Data Preview 1, interpreted with a Milky Way extinction curve.
AI.result: Detected a chromatic reddening profile from r_perp~10 kpc to 1 Mpc with A_V = (1.2±0.4)×10⁻¹ (r_perp/20 kpc)⁻¹·⁸±⁰·⁴ within 120 kpc. Innermost bin reaches A_V~0.3 mag. Red foreground galaxies show stronger extinction than blue ones. Dust-to-stellar-mass ratio ~1% for the red sample.
AI.conclusion: LSST's pathfinder data already reproduce established CGM dust measurements despite ~1000x smaller area and fainter foreground samples, confirming promise for future high-precision dust studies. The steep power-law slope suggests dust does not simply trace halo gas.
